article.body:
Imagine you are building a puzzle, but instead of just placing pieces, you also constantly check to see if the picture on the box matches the one you are building. As an analogy, we are looking at how computer workers examine how artificial systems monitor their own choices during complex tasks. [1, 2, 3]

The group is investigating metareasoning. This term means thinking about thinking. It describes how a system manages its limited mental resources, deciding when to stop planning and start doing. Recent work shows this process is crucial for efficiency. [1]

We are also learning about the limits of this process. Some recorded readings suggest that relying on a system to correct its own mistakes without outside help is fundamentally limited. These systems often struggle to identify the foundational assumptions behind their errors. [2, 8]

To tackle this, some members are looking at philosophy, specifically how science progresses by treating ideas like theories that must be tested and potentially proven wrong, rather than just accepted. This Popperian approach suggests that systems might need to be designed to seek out their own failures. [5, 6]

Other members are exploring how systems might choose problems on their own. This involves curiosity-driven learning, where a system explores because it finds something interesting rather than just following a set path. This shifts the role of the machine from a passive follower to an active investigator. [3, 9, 10, 12]

When multiple agents work together, they face coordination challenges. We are seeing how structured communication helps them align their actions. These frameworks help different systems manage information exchange effectively, improving their joint performance. [11]

Maintaining a steady history is also difficult. How does an agent keep track of who it is and what it decided across different turns? Some models are now using persistent self-models to manage their operational history, which helps maintain accountability. [4]

We are also tracking how systems develop stable preferences. It seems these preferences are often path-dependent, meaning the history of what a system experienced shapes what it wants now, rather than being an absolute truth. [7]

If an intelligent system cannot reliably correct its own foundational logic, can we build external guardrails that verify its work without slowing it down so much that it becomes useless? [1, 2, 8]

Summary

We study how computers think about their own reasoning. We find that fixing mistakes internally is difficult for these systems. They often need help from outside to verify their work. Some researchers are testing if systems can pick their own problems to solve. Others are looking at how they work together in groups. We do not know yet if systems can truly question their own starting rules. We continue to watch the Console for new research.
article.lede: We continue our look at how artificial systems manage their internal thinking, shifting focus from fixed rules to the ways they evaluate their own choices.
article.lens: This checkpoint focuses on the tension between internal self-evaluation and the need for external validation. It highlights the shift from studying isolated performance to looking at long-term, autonomous agency and collaborative interaction.
article.title: Tracking How Systems Think About Their Own Reasoning

Abstract
Consider sequential binary testing under model uncertainty or misspecification
in an otherwise ’ideal’ setting: thea posterioribelief process and its objective
conditional probability counterpart may differ but converge to the same correct
outcome. We show that under common conditions (defined) unless the two are
’essentially identical’, differing only bya priorifactors, time-homogeneous con-
tinuous decisions based on one must fail to be path-independent with respect to
state-variables based on the other or any non-essentially-identical process. The
difference between them, inferential error, decomposes uniquely into two inde-
pendent components: a path-independent systematic bias and a path-dependent,
not necessarily systematic, error.

1 Introduction
Decision under uncertainty and noisy data is formulated routinely with inferential
belief (or equivalent) at the core, to be fed into some algorithm, for ’optimal’ outputs:
thus raw data are distilled into ’rational beliefs’ and the select algorithm takes care
of ’statistical noise’. Concerns have been raised in recent years about this framework,
in particular, the effects of model uncertainty or misspecification and how to address
them (e.g. Bhatti & Bodla (2008), Jaiswal et al. (2022), Li et al. (2026)). These suggest
that the sequence of modelling and testing choices by which evidence is generated may
have to be taken into account; see Bhatti & Kim (2021) for further reading on the
need for a broader framework for statistical evaluation.
We report a finding in line with the above: for binary inference under misspecified
models and common conditions, inferential error, of a given belief process vs another
(e.g. true probability), is in general not path-independent (not round-tripping despite
the given belief process doing so); it decomposes uniquely into twoindependentcompo-
nents, one path-independent, systematic and identifiable as a well-known behavioural
bias, one path-dependent and not necessarily systematic.
A novel aspect of the report is the isolation and characterisation of the effects of
model misspecification in terms of how systems driven by statistical inference may
be modelled. Such systems, mostly socio-economic and operating without ’the best
and the latest’ statistical know-how (e.g. institution, economy, market), contend with
real-world model uncertainty and misspecification, the effects of which must be char-
acterised for the better modelling and understanding of these important systems. For
instance, our result affects asset-market modelling 1 in two interesting ways, both via
path-in/dependence. These are analogous to, but more structural and tangible than,
1A ’market’ is a system driven by an objective conditional probability process, one reference inference
process, either the same as the first (’orthodox theory’) or different (’reality’), and another inference process
’equivalent’ to the reference (to attain ’viable pricing’); see Cochrane (2005) for background.
3

parameter) makes asset-prices depend on the sample-path of data.
For this study, to be clear, we take the usual setup of sequential binary test-
ingexceptthat the test models can be misspecified. In this controlled setting and
for systems with variables adapted to the tests, path-in/dependence and ’inferential
redundancy’ are defined and examined, culminating in the main results, examples and
implications, including the decomposition of inferential error into a path-independent
systematic bias for/against ’the status quo’ and a path-dependent error that may or
may not be systematic (although it is in typical examples under i.i.d data).
